strengths: Clear and practical core insight that initial seed noise can be effectively optimized without full denoiser back-propagation, enabling training-free inpainting on off-the-shelf models
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across three standard benchmarks (FFHQ, DIV2K, BrushBench) with multiple metrics and consistent improvements over baselines (FLAIR, BrushNet)

Well-motivated technical contributions clearly articulated: linear approximation of denoising trajectories, spectral domain optimization for stability, and masked gradient updates to prevent artifacts
Effective ablation studies (Figures 5-6) demonstrating the necessity of each design choice, particularly the importance of spectral optimization and gradient masking
Extensive qualitative results with clear visualizations (Figures 7-10) showing competitive or superior inpainting quality across diverse image content
Practical training-free approach with clear method overview and implementation details
weaknesses: Limited theoretical analysis: linear approximation (Eq. 2) lacks error bounds or convergence guarantees; spectral optimization stability is explained intuitively but not rigorously formalized

Incremental core novelty: optimizing initial seed noise explored in concurrent work [35]; distinction unclear. Spectral filtering is straightforward; contribution is primarily the combination rather than fundamental innovation
Misleading framing of 'without back-propagation': nearest-neighbor fill-in followed by encoder gradient updates still constitutes partial back-propagation through the pipeline

Experimental evaluation gaps: no user studies (only model-based human preference metrics); limited mask diversity (primarily faces and rectangles, no medical imaging or complex object removal); scale limited to 1024×1024
Modest improvements over strong baselines: FID gains typically 2-3%; aesthetic score differences are small (e.g., Table 1: 6.233 vs 6.121); statistical significance not established

Critical methodological details relegated to implementation section (Section 3.4); VAE encoder assumption limiting applicability mentioned only briefly; lack of failure case analysis or method limitations discussion

Missing empirical analysis: no computational cost comparison; sensitivity to hyperparameters (optimization steps, learning rates) not studied; scalability and performance with larger/irregular masks unclear
Limited scope: only image inpainting; claimed potential for video/3D not demonstrated; tested only with Stable Diffusion variants; generalization to other diffusion models unclear

strengths: Well-motivated problem: clearly identifies and addresses the overlooked role of initial noise sample optimization in training-free diffusion-based inpainting

Theoretically grounded approach: rigorous linearization strategy (Eq. 2-3) avoiding expensive backpropagation, with formal proof (Section F.1) showing non-equivalence of spectral vs spatial optimization under adaptive optimizers

Comprehensive experimental validation: three datasets (FFHQ, DIV2K, BrushBench), multiple baselines, human preference study (90% preference, N=37 raters), quantitative metrics, and extensive ablations (Table 4) demonstrating necessity of each component

Practical training-free method: works with any pretrained diffusion model, comparable computational efficiency, generalizes to both flow-based and non-flow models, addressing real limitations of existing guidance methods
Strong empirical results: consistent improvements in SSIM, LPIPS, FID metrics; qualitative results demonstrate improved structural coherence; empirical validation of linearity assumption (Fig. 9)

Excellent presentation and thoroughness: clear motivation with effective visualizations, comprehensive supplementary material with additional analyses, user study details, and failure case discussions
weaknesses: Limited individual technical novelty: linearizing diffusion trajectories extends existing ideas, Adam optimization in spectral domain is straightforward application of existing optimizers; contribution primarily lies in combination rather than fundamental innovations

Theoretical assumptions not fully validated: linearity assumption (Eq. 2) assumes gradient term remains constant, but paper lacks thorough analysis of when this breaks down across different noise regimes and model architectures

Scope limitations: restricted to rectangular binary masks; generalization to arbitrary/irregular masks not demonstrated; video results preliminary and relegated to supplementary material; method specific to inpainting task
Image resolution constraints: limited to 1024×1024 images due to computational bottlenecks; scalability to higher resolutions unclear

Experimental concerns: hyperparameters appear tuned for this method without sensitivity analysis; PSNR sometimes lower than baselines (Tables 1-3); some evaluation metrics show mixed results (CLIP score inconsistent); guidance scale choices for baselines not fully justified

Incomplete reproducibility: no code availability mentioned as major limitation; VAE masking details unclear; hyperparameter selection process undocumented; some implementation aspects (latent space updates) need clarification

Limited failure analysis: paper mentions but does not deeply explore failure cases; no analysis of when optimization might hurt performance; convergence failure modes of spatial Adam (Fig. 12) not thoroughly explained

Incremental improvements: while consistent, improvements over FLAIR and other baselines are sometimes modest in specific metrics; trained methods (BrushNet) remain competitive on some datasets, limiting practical advantage
